questions.q: Define the profit-maximization condition for a monopolistically competitive firm in the short run and state the relationship between price and marginal cost at that equilibrium.
questions.a: Correct answer: The firm maximizes profit where MR = MC. Because the demand curve is downward sloping, MR < P, so at the MR = MC output, P > MC. A wrong answer stating P = MC reveals confusion with perfect competition; stating P = MR reveals confusion with monopoly (where MR < P also holds, but the student may not recognize that monopolistic competition shares this feature). The key is recognizing that product differentiation gives market power, so price exceeds marginal cost.

questions.q: Explain why the long-run equilibrium of a monopolistically competitive firm results in zero economic profit but not minimum average cost. Use the concepts of free entry/exit and product differentiation.
questions.a: Correct answer: Free entry eliminates supernormal profits by shifting each firm's demand curve left until it is tangent to the AC curve (P = AC, zero economic profit). Product differentiation makes the demand curve downward sloping, so tangency occurs on the falling portion of the U-shaped AC curve, not at its minimum. A wrong answer claiming long-run equilibrium occurs at min AC confuses monopolistic competition with perfect competition. A wrong answer claiming firms earn supernormal profits in the long run ignores free entry. The student must link the shape of the demand curve (downward sloping due to differentiation) to the tangency point.

questions.q: A monopolistically competitive firm faces demand P = 200 - 0.5Q and has total cost TC = 2000 + 40Q. Calculate the short-run profit-maximizing output, price, and profit. Show all steps.
questions.a: Step 1: TR = P×Q = (200 - 0.5Q)Q = 200Q - 0.5Q². Step 2: MR = d(TR)/dQ = 200 - Q. Step 3: MC = d(TC)/dQ = 40. Step 4: Set MR = MC → 200 - Q = 40 → Q* = 160 units. Step 5: P* = 200 - 0.5(160) = ₹120. Step 6: TR = 120×160 = ₹19,200. TC = 2000 + 40×160 = ₹8,400. Profit = ₹19,200 - ₹8,400 = ₹10,800 (supernormal). A wrong answer using P = MC gives Q = 320, P = 40, loss = -₹2,000 — this is the competitive outcome, not monopolistic competition. A wrong answer setting MR = 0 gives Q = 200 (revenue max), not profit max.

questions.q: Compare the long-run equilibrium outcomes of monopolistic competition and perfect competition on three dimensions: (a) price vs marginal cost, (b) output relative to minimum efficient scale, (c) product variety. Explain the economic intuition for each difference.
questions.a: Correct answer: (a) Monopolistic competition: P > MC (markup due to market power); perfect competition: P = MC. (b) Monopolistic competition: output < min AC (excess capacity); perfect competition: output = min AC (productive efficiency). (c) Monopolistic competition: differentiated products provide variety valued by consumers; perfect competition: homogeneous products, no variety. Intuition: Product differentiation creates downward-sloping demand, giving firms pricing power (P > MC) and causing them to operate on the falling part of AC. Free entry drives profit to zero but not to min AC. A wrong answer stating both have P = MC misses the markup. A wrong answer stating monopolistic competition achieves min AC ignores the tangency condition on a downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Monopolistic competition is socially wasteful because firms operate with excess capacity and charge P > MC. The government should force all firms to produce at minimum average cost." Consider both efficiency and consumer welfare perspectives.
questions.a: Correct answer: The statement overlooks the benefit of product variety. Excess capacity and P > MC represent allocative and productive inefficiency, but consumers gain from differentiated products that match diverse preferences. Forcing production at min AC would require standardizing products (like perfect competition), eliminating variety. The net welfare effect is ambiguous: the deadweight loss from markup must be weighed against the consumer surplus from variety. A good evaluation acknowledges the trade-off. A wrong answer agreeing fully ignores consumer valuation of differentiation; a wrong answer dismissing inefficiency entirely ignores the real resource cost of excess capacity.

questions.q: Construct a numerical example where a monopolistically competitive firm in long-run equilibrium has demand P = a - bQ and cost TC = F + cQ. Choose parameters a, b, c, F such that the long-run tangency condition holds (P = AC and MR = MC at the same Q). Show the equilibrium output, price, and verify zero profit.
questions.a: Let demand: P = 100 - Q (so a=100, b=1). Cost: TC = 400 + 20Q (F=400, c=20). MR = 100 - 2Q. MC = 20. Set MR=MC: 100-2Q=20 → Q*=40. P* = 100-40 = 60. AC = 400/40 + 20 = 30. Not tangent (P=60 ≠ AC=30). Adjust F to achieve tangency. At tangency, demand is tangent to AC → slope of demand = slope of AC at Q*. Slope of demand = -1. AC = F/Q + 20. d(AC)/dQ = -F/Q². Set -F/Q² = -1 → F = Q². Also P = AC → 100 - Q = F/Q + 20. Substitute F=Q²: 100 - Q = Q + 20 → 80 = 2Q → Q*=40. Then F = 1600. Check: TC = 1600 + 20Q. At Q=40: AC = 1600/40+20=60=P. MR=100-80=20=MC. Profit = (60-60)×40=0. Parameters: a=100, b=1, c=20, F=1600. A poor answer fails to impose both tangency conditions simultaneously or chooses parameters that don't satisfy MR=MC and P=AC at the same Q.
